companies.thesis: CHRW is the cleanest realized AI-operational-efficiency story in freight brokerage: a genuinely decoupled headcount/volume curve backed by a mechanism-specific, monotonically improving productivity-per-head metric explicitly credited to generative AI. Across all five of the last five quarters, average NAST headcount fell 11-13% YoY while volume held flat-to-up, and shipments per person per day rose from +30% (Q1'25) to +50%+ (Q1'26) since 2022, driving NAST operating margin from 34.3% (Q1'25) to ~39% (Q3'25) and +310bps YoY ex-restructuring in both Q4'25 and Q1'26. Management substantiates the AI attribution with hard throughput numbers (LTL-classification agent: 10 min to 10 sec on ~2,000 orders/day; 95% of missed-pickup checks automated, 350 hours/day saved; RFQ cycle 17-20 min to 32 seconds) rather than slogans. The main caveat: the headcount reductions carry recurring restructuring charges and a 'lean' baseline, so AI is the incremental productivity offset on top of a deliberate RIF, not the sole driver.
companies.evidence_detail:

Q2 2025: LTL freight-classification AI agent determines class/code for ~2,000 orders/day, cutting processing from 10+ min to 10 sec/shipment. Productivity +35% since 2022; avg headcount -11.2% YoY; NAST operating margin ~38%; NAST gross margin +80bps YoY.

Q3 2025: 450+ in-house engineers/data scientists; fleet of AI agents across quote-to-cash plus an 'always-on logistics planner' with 30+ connected agents, scaling only on token cost (no incremental tech spend). Productivity +40% since 2022 (NAST), +55% Global Forwarding; avg headcount -10.8% YoY decoupled from +3% volume; NAST adjusted operating margin 39%.

Q4 2025: 30+ custom AI agents deployed; 95% of missed-LTL-pickup checks automated (350 hrs/day saved, 42% fewer return trips); RFQ completion 60%->100% and cycle 17-20 min -> 32 sec. NAST operating margin +310bps YoY ex-restructuring (company +320bps); avg headcount -12.9% YoY; shipments/person +40%+ since 2022, double-digit for FY2025.

Q1 2026: Shipments per person per day now >50% higher than 2022; double-digit NAST productivity again in Q1. Avg headcount -12.3% YoY; personnel expense (ex-restructuring) -$13.4M / -3.9% YoY; NAST operating margin +310bps YoY; company operating margin +210bps YoY; total NAST volume flat vs CAS index -6.2%.
companies.risks: Attribution entanglement is the core risk: headcount cuts carry recurring restructuring charges (e.g., $9.7M Q3'25, $3.9M Q2'25), so margin gains are quoted 'ex-restructuring' and AI is the productivity offset on top of a deliberate RIF plus a 'single-digit-per-year' lean baseline — AI is the incremental delta, not the whole gain. Gross-margin improvements (+140/+80/+70/+20bps) partly reflect pricing/contract-mix (contractual TL rose to ~70%) and spot-rate spread, not AI. The gains are occurring during a prolonged freight recession (CAS -6% to -8% YoY); an up-cycle could change the cost dynamics and lap increasingly tough productivity comps (already +50% since 2022), risking deceleration, and part of the 2026 guide is 'over-indexed to H2,' i.e. still forward promise. Management is heavily promoting a 'Lean AI'/AgenTeq narrative, so some AI-washing risk exists — but the specific per-head throughput metrics are hard and verifiable, which keeps it well above washing. Attribution is management's framing, not an independently decomposable fact. The headline margin expansion (34.3%->~39%; +310bps YoY) is driven primarily by an 11-13% YoY headcount reduction — a deliberate RIF carrying recurring restructuring charges — and "shipments per person per day" is a ratio that rises mechanically as heads are cut, whether or not AI did the cutting. Management never quantifies the AI share vs. RIF/process discipline, so "explicitly credited to generative AI" means credited by the CEO/CFO, not verified as AI-caused. Second, the productivity % (30/35/40/50%) is cumulative off a fixed 2022 base, so the quarter-over-quarter "acceleration" partly reflects a receding base year, not necessarily faster AI adoption. Third, NAST gross-margin/AGP moves also reflect truckload buy-sell spreads in a soft freight cycle — margin attribution to AI is looser than the (genuinely strong) task-throughput attribution. Net: the mechanism anecdotes are real and specific, which is why this survives; but the thesis should not treat management's AI credit for the aggregate margin/productivity numbers as independently proven.

companies.thesis: XPO shows a genuine, realized, unusually durable AI-operational-efficiency signal: management has reported an AI-attributed labor-productivity gain in each of the last five quarters, accelerating as proprietary tools roll out network-wide — +1 pt (Q1'25), ~1 pt (Q2'25), +2.5 pts hours/shipment (Q3'25), +2 pts (Q4'25), +4% (Q1'26 vs a 1.5% long-term target). Critically, gains persisted as volumes fell (tonnage −7.5% Q1'25; shipments −3.5% / tonnage −6.1% Q3'25), a counter-cyclical decoupling management ties to AI route optimization (linehaul miles −3%, empty miles >10%, diversions >80%, more stops/hour), automated door-loading (shipments/trailer +low-single-digits), and AI trailer-load tools (damage claims to a record <0.2%). This supports adjusted-OR expansion that beat seasonality (+150-300bps YoY across 2025; +30bps sequential in Q1'25), with each productivity point worth ~$25-30M EBITDA. Caveats: OR expansion is also driven materially by pricing (yield ex-fuel ~+7%), and the AI-specific magnitude is management-attributed and not independently separable from ordinary down-cycle cost discipline. The headline "purchased transportation −46-53%" is linehaul INSOURCING, not AI, and should be discounted.
companies.evidence_detail:
Q1 2025: +1% improvement in hours per shipment despite tonnage down 7.5% YoY, attributed to proprietary tech that flexes labor in real time + newly deployed AI-driven linehaul models; adjusted OR +30bps to 85.9% beating seasonality

Q2 2025: ~1% labor productivity gain; AI models cut normalized linehaul miles ~3%, empty miles >10%, diversions >80%; P&D AI route-optimization piloted at 4 terminals with positive stops/hour; adjusted OR +300bps sequentially to 82.9%

Q3 2025: Labor hours per shipment improved +2.5 points even as shipments fell ~6 pts YoY, explicitly attributed to AI optimizing linehaul/dock/pickup; automated door-loading lifted shipments/trailer low-single-digits; adjusted OR +150bps YoY to 82.7%

Q4 2025: +2 points labor productivity in Q4 (~1.5 pts full year with H2 ramp from tech rollouts); AI P&D route-optimization pilot completed across 12 service centers with each point of P&D efficiency worth ~$9M/yr; expanding to ~half of service centers; adjusted OR +180bps

Q1 2026: Productivity +4%, well above the 1.5% long-term target, with AI P&D route tools now on ~half the network (full by year-end) and AI trailer-load tools driving damage claims to a record <0.2%; each productivity point ~$25-30M incremental EBITDA; adjusted OR +200bps YoY to 83.9%
companies.risks: Attribution/confound: the single largest and most-cited cost number — purchased transportation down 46-53% YoY — is primarily linehaul insourcing (outsourced miles cut from ~9% to 5.1%), a vertical-integration decision, not AI efficiency; crediting it to AI (as the prior note did) overstates the case. OR/margin expansion is also entangled with strong LTL pricing and a freight-recession cost-out narrative, so the AI leg cannot be cleanly isolated in GAAP margins. The "productivity points" and the $9M- and $25-30M-per-point EBITDA sensitivities are management-defined, self-reported figures, not audited line items. Promotional risk is elevated — freight management leans hard into "AI" branding — though XPO backs it with specific mechanisms and a credible staged network rollout. Reversibility risk: some productivity in a down-volume environment reflects network rationalization that could unwind on a demand recovery, though the accelerating trend as tools scale argues against pure cyclicality. Attribution risk is the core weakness: every AI-productivity figure is management self-reported with no external audit, and cannot be cleanly separated from headcount reduction in a soft freight market, network rationalization, or the standard LTL efficiency playbook — "AI" is a convenient label on gains that would partly occur anyway. Much of the OR beat is pricing/yield (ex-fuel yield ~+7%), not AI. Productivity-per-shipment can also flatter mechanically when weight-per-shipment falls. The signal is real and recurring but its dollar quantification ($9M/P&D point, $25-30M/productivity point) is a management framework, not a booked, verifiable P&L line. Durability depends on continued rollout execution (P&D tools only ~half deployed) and holds only while the freight cycle stays soft enough to keep productivity the growth story.

companies.thesis: FactSet has a genuine, mechanism-specific, AI-attributed internal-efficiency story that has escalated across three consecutive quarters. By Q3 FY2026 (May 2026), CEO Sanoke Viswanathan stated AI coding agents author ~27% of committed code on participating teams (up from ~20% in Q2 FY2026), and management explicitly attributed a ~10% reduction in the technology workforce to AI-assisted coding productivity. Data operations show concrete headcount decoupling: 10x faster third-party data ingestion "without adding headcount" (Q1 FY2026), >25% average cuts in manual curation from four AI tools (Q2 FY2026), and >50% lower operator touch time plus a 5% Fundamentals-team reduction (Q3 FY2026). Management claims it captured >50% of a targeted 100 bps of FY2026 productivity improvement in the first half. This is stronger than a plan, but it falls short of the cleanest "realized" names because reported adjusted operating margin actually FELL to ~34% (from 36.8% YoY) as AI-infrastructure spend and higher performance comp more than offset the savings — the efficiency is being reinvested, not yet visible on the bottom line.
companies.evidence_detail:
Q4 FY2025: Internal AI framed qualitatively only (redeploying talent, faster CallStreet); AI disclosed mainly as a client-facing revenue lever (~40 bps ASV midpoint contribution). No quantified internal-efficiency metrics — the baseline before the efficiency narrative ramped.

Q1 FY2026: Text-to-formula agent handles ~35% of daily formula-support questions (resolving in ~6 seconds vs minutes); data operations ingests third-party data at 10x speed 'without adding headcount' — first quantified internal-efficiency/headcount-decoupling metrics.

Q2 FY2026: AI coding tools author ~20% of successful code commits and free ~25% of engineers' capacity on participating teams; four AI tools cut manual data-curation work by >25% on average; company reports it captured >50% of its targeted 100 bps of FY2026 productivity improvement in H1.

Q3 FY2026: AI agents author ~27% of committed code (AI-committed lines ~10x QoQ, coding tokens 5x QoQ); ~10% technology-workforce reduction explicitly attributed to AI-assisted coding productivity; operator touch time for data extraction down >50%; Fundamentals team cut 5%; overall headcount down ~1%.

Q3 FY2026: Despite the efficiency actions, adjusted operating margin fell to ~34% (from 36.8% YoY) — attributed to AI-infrastructure investment and higher performance comp — showing the AI savings are being reinvested rather than expanding margins.
companies.risks: Attribution ambiguity: the ~10% tech-workforce cut coincides with a new CEO (Sanoke Viswanathan, ex-JPMorgan, in seat under a year) — a classic restructuring/cost-discipline confound dressed as AI, and the prior note's attribution to "Phil Snow" was wrong (Snow retired). Bottom-line invisibility: adjusted operating margin actually COMPRESSED (~34% vs 36.8% YoY), so the efficiency is real at the activity level but is being consumed by AI-infra spend and comp — it is NOT yet a demonstrable margin tailwind, unlike cleaner realized names. Promotional/measurement risk: "% of code authored by AI" and "% of engineer capacity freed" are self-reported, hard-to-audit engineering vanity metrics; the 100 bps productivity target is management-defined. Durability is only ~3 quarters old and reversibility is real if a hiring rebound follows. Finally, FactSet's AI narrative is heavily weighted toward AI as a revenue product, which can blur the internal-efficiency signal. Add three risks the deep-dive under-weights: (1) Attribution incentive — management has a self-serving reason to badge a ~10% technology-workforce layoff as "AI productivity" rather than cost discipline or macro; the AI causation is management's framing and is not independently auditable. (2) Scope inflation — the 27% code-commit and 25% capacity figures are on "teams using these tools" / "participating teams," a self-selected subset, and overstate enterprise-wide impact; company-wide code authorship is unstated and lower. (3) No bottom-line proof — adjusted operating margin fell ~280 bps YoY to 34%, so the efficiency remains invisible to shareholders; if reinvestment persists, the "realized" savings never convert to earnings, weakening the case for the "realized" label vs a "reinvested/in-progress" one.

companies.thesis: Hinge Health is a genuine REALIZED AI-efficiency name, not AI-washing: the benefit is already visible in the P&L and is mechanism-specific. The cleanest datapoint is the care-team decoupling — the company served 47% more members in 2025 while holding care-team costs flat, and guided care-team headcount flat-to-down again in 2026 despite growing revenue, driven by AI-automated clinician workflows (its model "automates over 95% of clinician hours associated with traditional PT"). This shows up as consistent gross-margin expansion (77%->83% in Q2'25, 79%->83% in Q3'25, 82%->85% in Q4'25, 81%->85% in Q1'26, all attributed to care-team efficiency "largely enabled by AI-powered tools") and large operating-margin gains. Crucially, CFO James Budge explicitly quantified attribution on the Q3'25 call: of ~2,600bps of combined margin improvement, "a good half of that came from AI advances." The evidence is durable across all four quarters the company has reported as a public company.
companies.evidence_detail:

Q3 2025: CFO James Budge (Q&A): of ~2,600bps combined gross+operating margin improvement YoY, "a good half of that came from AI advances." Gross margin 83% vs 79%; operating margin 20% vs -4%; operating income $30M.

Q3 2025: AI raised engineering output: code output +120% and features shipped 3x faster vs Q3'24; engineer AI adoption ~20%->~100%. Care-team headcount guided "roughly flat to down" in 2026 despite rising revenue.

Q4 2025: Served 47% more members in 2025 while keeping care-team costs flat; clinician async session time fell 28% from Q3 to Q4 via AI-automated messaging; Robin AI assistant 92% positive rating. Gross margin 85% vs 82%; operating margin 28% vs 18%; operating income $48M; FY25 op margin 20% vs -7% in 2024.

Q1 2026: Operating margin 25% vs 12% (+~1,300bps YoY), operating income $46M; gross margin 85% vs 81% (+400bps) on care-team/hardware efficiency + AI/automation; opex ratio 60% vs 69% of revenue; CFO: AI "increased efficiency across all operating categories," driving slower-than-planned hiring. Model "automates over 95% of clinician hours" vs traditional PT.
companies.risks: Attribution is partly a management estimate, not independently verifiable: the CFO himself concedes only ~half of the 2,600bps margin swing came from AI — the rest is ordinary post-IPO scale operating leverage, and margins are reported non-GAAP/adjusted (FY24 -7% to FY25 +20% is a large swing that flatters the AI narrative). Track record is thin: HNGE has only ~4 quarters of public reporting (IPO May 2025), so durability beyond one year is unproven. Promotional risk is elevated — a newly public digital-health name has strong incentive to over-attribute margin to AI, and the sector has a history of hype (Teladoc, etc.). The flashier "code output +120% / 3x faster" figure is R&D productivity, not a realized P&L line. Reversibility risk: "flat care team" leverage may not hold if member acuity or growth mix shifts, or if competition compresses pricing; and because AI is intrinsic to care delivery, the line between operating efficiency and product economics is blurred. All cited profit/margin figures are NON-GAAP; GAAP results still show large operating losses (Q2'25 -$580.7M, FY25 -$546.4M) driven overwhelmingly by post-IPO stock-based compensation — real economic dilution the thesis sidesteps by leaning on non-GAAP. Attribution is largely self-reported: the "a good half came from AI" and "automates 95% of clinician hours" figures are management characterizations, not independently auditable, and gross-margin gains are also driven by hardware-cost efficiency and scale (management itself lists "care-team/hardware efficiency + AI/automation" jointly in Q1'26), so AI is a major but not sole driver. Only four quarters of public data — durability is asserted over a short window.

companies.thesis: Robinhood has a genuine, quantified, AI-attributed operational-efficiency story concentrated in two functions: customer support and software engineering. In Q4 2025 management disclosed that over 75% of support cases are now resolved by AI — including complex cases that previously required licensed brokerage professionals — producing "estimated 9-figure" (~$100M+) real savings in 2025, a figure reaffirmed in Q1 2026. The most compelling proof is mechanism-specific and shows up in the financials: 2025 volumes grew ~50% while customer-service hiring stayed roughly flat (volume/headcount decoupling), code commits per engineer rose ~50% since the start of 2025, and >90% of employees now use AI tooling — all while OpEx grew low-single-digits and adjusted EBITDA margins expanded past 56%. This clears the realized bar, but the hard dollar figure is a single annual management estimate (disclosed Q4 2025, reaffirmed Q1 2026), and the margin expansion is partly cyclical operating leverage on a fixed cost base rather than pure AI.
companies.evidence_detail:
Q1 2025: Qualitative only: Tenev says the company is 'improving the operations of the company and also the customer service through AI'; most AI commentary is about Cortex, a customer-facing product, not internal efficiency. No quantified internal savings.

Q2 2025: AI called 'critical' and 'world-class' in engineering and customer service; credited as 'a big part of why we've been able to demonstrate this growth while keeping OpEx relatively flat' — ~56% adj. EBITDA margin on +45% YoY revenue. No AI-specific dollar figure disclosed.

Q3 2025: 'Best-in-class' AI in customer service and engineering reiterated; specific metrics deferred to a future AI event. No quantified figures on the call.

Q4 2025: 'Over 75% of our cases are solved by AI, including the complex cases that previously required licensed brokerage professionals'; 'real savings and efficiency gains estimated at 9 figures in 2025 alone' (~$100M+); engineering pipeline automated from coding to deployment/testing; 85-90% of costs fixed.

Q1 2026: CFO reaffirms '$100M in efficiency, primarily in CX and software engineering'; code commits per engineer at a new high, up ~50% since start of 2025; >90% of employees using AI tooling; 2025 volumes grew ~50% while customer-service hiring stayed roughly flat (headcount/volume decoupling).
companies.risks: Attribution is the central risk: the ~$100M figure is management's own estimate ("estimated at 9 figures"), not an auditable line item, and 2025 revenue nearly doubled on an 85-90% fixed cost base — so much of the margin expansion is cyclical operating leverage that would occur with or without AI, making it hard to isolate the AI contribution. Durability of the hard number is thin: it is one annual figure disclosed in Q4 2025 and reaffirmed once in Q1 2026, not five independent quarterly datapoints (Q1-Q3 2025 were qualitative). Promotional risk is elevated — Tenev is a hype-forward CEO ("best in the world," "push every team to integrate AI") and Robinhood also markets Cortex, an AI revenue product, which can blur internal-efficiency messaging. Finally, part of the "efficiency" is volume absorption during a crypto/options up-cycle; a volume downturn would preserve headcount savings but weaken the growth-decoupling narrative. Add three risks the deep-dive underweights: (1) The ~$100M is cost-AVOIDANCE, not cost reduction — gross OpEx still rose; the figure represents hiring Robinhood believes it avoided, an inherently counterfactual, un-auditable management estimate with no disclosed methodology, disclosed once and reaffirmed once. (2) The volume/headcount decoupling rode a 2025 crypto/trading-volume boom (~+50% volumes); a favorable cyclical surge flatters "flat CS hiring per unit volume," and an 85-90% fixed-cost base that looks like leverage in an up-cycle becomes a margin drag in a downturn — the efficiency story is partly indistinguishable from operating leverage on a cyclical high. (3) The "75% of cases solved by AI" metric is management-defined and unaudited (deflection vs. true end-to-end resolution is not specified), so the headline automation rate may overstate genuine displacement of licensed staff.

Net: genuine realized efficiency, but the strongest "savings" number is partly non-AI and the productivity denominators are distorted by M&A and refi-cycle tailwinds.

companies.risks: Attribution is the core risk: the two largest 'savings' numbers are confounded — the $80M run-rate is half business wind-downs/restructuring, and the loans-per-team-member gains are inflated by both a refi-volume recovery (productivity-per-head rises mechanically in any mortgage upcycle) and the Mr. Cooper/Redfin acquisitions that reshape the headcount and volume denominators (the $400M Mr. Cooper and $140M Redfin synergies are integration, not AI). (3) The comms-engine ">$1B incremental volume/month" is a top-line attribution/marketing figure, not a verified cost saving, and should not be counted toward operational-efficiency realization. companies.thesis: Navan clears the realized bar on one clean, mechanism-specific channel: its Ava virtual agent now handles/deflects ~54-55% of customer interactions (Q3 FY26 54% deflection; Q4 FY26 55% handled, incl. 55% of winter-storm inquiries resolved without a human), and management repeatedly and explicitly attributes gross-margin expansion to that support automation — CFO Butte naming "continued automation of customer support through Ava," and CEO Cohen quantifying "over 1,000 basis points of gross margin expansion over the last two fiscal years." Because customer support sits in a TMC's COGS, this is a genuine AI-to-P&L linkage, not AI-washing and not an AI revenue product. Caveat: the gross-margin gain cannot be cleanly isolated from scale leverage in COGS, and the +870-1,100bps operating-margin jumps are largely scale, not AI. Two supporting specifics in the source note (Q1 "10x faster / a fraction the cost," Q3 "~80% satisfaction") are unverifiable and should be dropped.

companies.thesis: Ingram Micro has delivered five consecutive quarters of operating-expense-leverage improvement that management explicitly and repeatedly attributes to "optimization and automation" from its Xvantage digital platform. CFO Michael Zilis quantified opex falling to 4.41% of net sales in Q4 FY2025 (a 74 bps YoY improvement from 5.15%) and 47 bps of FY2025 opex leverage, with 17-20 bps of YoY improvement in Q2/Q3 2025 and 12 bps of SG&A leverage in Q1 2026; CEO Paul Bay adds that in the lead Xvantage country "overall headcount has decreased" while revenue and gross profit per go-to-market head rose. The mechanism is genuine (touchless generative-AI "email-to-order," self-service, the IDA assistant lowering cost-to-serve). However, the AI-attributed portion is never isolated from ordinary "optimization," scale, and a one-off insurance recovery, so this is a realized-but-heavily-entangled case rather than a clean AI-efficiency proof.
companies.evidence_detail:

Q3 2025: Operating expenses 5.13% of net sales (SG&A 5.10%) vs 5.33% prior year, ~20 bps YoY improvement, which management said reflects 'improved operating expense leverage following our optimization and automation efforts.'

Q4 2025: CFO Michael Zilis: Q4 opex $656.7M = 4.41% of net sales vs 5.15%, a 74 bps YoY improvement that 'reflects the continued benefits of optimization and automation from Xvantage, as well as a positive recovery via insurance proceeds' (i.e. partly a non-AI one-off); FY2025 opex 5% of sales, +47 bps.

Q4 2025: CEO Paul Bay: 'In the largest country where we have rolled out Xvantage, overall headcount has decreased, and the revenue and gross profit per go-to-market head have increased' — a headcount/output decoupling attributed to the platform (unquantified).

Q1 2026: Opex 5.04% of net sales; SG&A improved to 4.97% from 5.10% (12 bps YoY) amid net sales +13.7%; generative-AI email-to-order hit 230,000 conversions (+78% YoY) and 2.0M+ self-service orders, framed as cost-to-serve reduction.
companies.risks: Attribution is the core weakness: management always bundles "optimization AND automation," never isolating the AI-specific bps, so an unknown share is ordinary cost discipline and recurring restructuring charges. The cleanest figure (Q4's 74 bps) is explicitly polluted by an insurance recovery and offsetting reserves, making it non-repeatable. The bigger confound is scale — net sales grew 7-14% YoY every quarter while opex dollars also rose (Q1'26 opex +$75M/+12%), so much of the falling opex ratio is a denominator/operating-leverage effect from volume, not AI. Finally, most of INGM's headline "AI" (AI-led net sales +60%, AI-infrastructure deal mix, $1B+ email-to-order GMV) is a revenue story, not internal efficiency, and the genuine efficiency claims (headcount decoupling) remain unquantified. Separately, opex-as-a-percent-of-sales declines partly as an arithmetic consequence of 8-14% net-sales growth (operating leverage on a rising denominator), so an unquantified but likely material portion of every quarter's 'leverage' is scale and mix, not AI. 'Optimization and automation' also bundles conventional headcount restructuring with Xvantage automation, and Xvantage is a broad digital/e-commerce platform of which only part is genuinely AI.

Net: a credible, articulated, partially-proven AI-efficiency plan with early operational realization, but the in-the-numbers benefit remains entangled with restructuring and offshoring, so it falls short of the clean, multi-quarter, AI-attributed-P&L standard for REALIZED.

BUT the efficiency is NOT yet in the financials as AI-attributed margin: "hours saved" is an unmonetized productivity proxy with no headcount or cost decoupling, the headline 44% "conversion lift" is a revenue metric (savings-account conversions), expenses still grew +12% partly BECAUSE of AI investment, and management's own 3.6-4% positive operating leverage (10th-11th consecutive quarter) is explicitly NOT attributed to AI and long predates the AI ramp. CFO Sedran: "AI is not pixie dust. It requires investment." This is a credible, quantified AI-productivity plan in mid-deployment — not a realized P&L benefit.

companies.risks: Attribution/monetization gap is the core red flag: "hours saved" is an unmonetized input proxy — CIBC discloses NO headcount reduction, G&A leverage, or margin bps cleanly attributed to AI, and expenses are still growing +12% partly because of AI spend, so AI is currently a net cost in the P&L. near_misses.headline: CEO disclaimed his own AI number in the next sentence

quotes.q: anywhere from a 30 to 40% decrease in cycle time from a coding perspective.
Now that's really not a savings because what that does is allows us to do more.
a lack of acceleration in hiring of more travel representatives, more customer service reps, even as the business continues to grow

near_misses.kill: The CEO removes his own headline from contention one sentence later: the coding gain is recycled into backlog throughput, not harvested as cost. The financials agree — total expenses +12.3% on revenue +10.0%, opex ratio 150bp WORSE year over year, and 62% of the pretax increase comes from a $321mm provision release. The metric definition also drifted in a single quarter, from Q1's '30% benefit... coding and testing' to Q2's '30–40% decrease in cycle time... coding'.
near_misses.survives: Management does attribute flat servicing hiring to AI tools — explicit, correctly ordered attribution. But it arrives with no rep count, no baseline and no cost figure. Attribution without quantification is a lead, not evidence.
near_misses.materiality: Most generous construction: ~$23mm quarterly, 0.16% of the $14,482mm expense base — below the 0.5% floor.
near_misses.watch: Q3 2026: if servicing headcount actually declines as Squeri predicts AND the opex ratio inflects below 72%, re-open with a quantified basis. Otherwise hard reject.

near_misses.headline: Richest AI disclosure of the quarter; unit costs went the wrong way

quotes.q: Using our new AI tools, we reduced the time required by 97%.
It has now processed more than 50,000 orders, delivering 92% with no additional human review.
We have also improved automation rates from 30% in Q1 to 34% in Q2, and so far in July, we are at 39%.

near_misses.kill: Revenue rose 15% on a 17.3% lift in revenue per order while order counts were FLAT to DOWN (closes 2,145/day vs 2,161). Title firms staff to order count but bill on order value, so price and commercial mix compress the expense ratio with zero productivity gain. Opex per closed order actually ROSE ~10.6% and personnel per order ~8.4%. The 97% covers a one-time 1,300-form template update. Management's own success ratio MISSED at 66% against a 60% target.
near_misses.survives: Endpoint's 30%→34%→39% series is genuinely consistently defined across two quarters — the single best piece of evidence in the file. The title-plant data moat is a credible mechanism.
near_misses.materiality: Every AI figure is an activity metric with no dollar or headcount attached. Exam Assist's 50,000 cumulative orders is ~36% of ONE quarter's direct closes; Endpoint's 39% applies to one converted branch, with network rollout not due until end-2027.
near_misses.peer: Stewart (STC) improved employee costs from 29.5% to 27.4% of revenue — 210bp, BETTER than FAF's 201bp — with no AI attribution anywhere. Same driver at both: commercial mix.
near_misses.watch: FNF, the decisive comparable, reports 2026-08-05. Re-scan after it prints and after two more Endpoint datapoints on a stable definition.

near_misses.headline: Management's own margin bridge omits the AI tool

quotes.q: Lily, our AI voice assistant, now handles approximately 20% of our inbound service calls from start to finish, with performance exceeding 30% during certain periods.
intelligent case routing, which has allowed us to reinvest roughly 40 full-time service team members towards more complex and value-added interactions
comp and G&A to grow in the high teens to low 20% for the year, which will likely be in excess of core revenue growth

near_misses.kill: Management bridged 30% adjusted EBITDA growth to retention of 86%, new business, carrier commission dynamics and bind rates — and did not mention AI. When management lists its own margin bridge and omits the tool, the analyst does not get to add it. The CFO then guided comp and G&A to grow AHEAD of core revenue, which is the opposite of harvesting service automation. The metric definition also narrowed: Q1's 'all inbound calls' became Q2's 'inbound service calls', mechanically inflating the ratio, so 19%→20% may be flat or down like-for-like.
near_misses.survives: The peer check FAILS to kill it — Brown & Brown's margin went the other way (EBITDAC 35.7% vs 36.7%), so there is no sector tailwind explaining GSHD away. Its expansion is company-specific. The mechanism is also genuinely credible: 2.1m policies in force and labour-intensive personal-lines service calls are exactly where voice AI works.
near_misses.materiality: The 40 redeployed FTEs are ~$4.9mm, ~1.7% of FY2025 opex — but they were REINVESTED, not removed. Realized disclosed saving: $0. Headcount leverage also predates Lily's deployment.
near_misses.watch: Q3 2026: one disclosure — service headcount against policies in force, or cost per service interaction, on a stable definition — would put this into scoring range quickly.

near_misses.headline: Real AI saving, honestly disclosed, roughly two orders of magnitude too small to reach the financials

quotes.q: Even our legal department has several high ROI adjunctive use cases in production.
including one agent that reviews invoices from outside counsel firms and now saves us a point and a half in our legal bills every month
reflecting continued discipline and scale, as well as product mix.

near_misses.kill: The saving is 1.5% of an undisclosed sub-line-item — outside counsel spend, which appears nowhere in Centene's income statement — so it is structurally unverifiable and bounds to roughly $1.5–$15mm a year, 0.01–0.12% of annualised SG&A. Management's own bridge explains the 20bp adjusted SG&A improvement (7.1% → 6.9%) twice without AI: the CFO cites "continued discipline and scale, as well as product mix", and the release cites "leveraging of expenses over higher revenues and reduced Marketplace membership, which operates at a meaningfully higher SG&A expense ratio". The unit-cost test is fatal — membership fell 7.6% (28.00mm → 25.89mm) while SG&A dollars ROSE $67mm to $3,103mm, so SG&A per member per month rose from $36.14 to $39.96, +10.6% (+20.6% ex-PDP). The ratio fell only because revenue per member rose 13.0%. The real SG&A lever is a $480mm workforce and enterprise optimisation programme that management never attributes to AI.
near_misses.survives: The mechanism is genuine and the disclosure is unusually restrained — outside-counsel e-billing review is a mature, auditable AI application, and London volunteered a hard percentage while calling the use cases "adjunctive" and describing AI deployed "selectively, with a strong focus on return on investment rather than broad experimentation". No revenue conflation. CNC was also the only managed-care name in the peer set to improve its ratio at all (UNH +40bp, ELV +100bp, MOH +50bp) — but that gap is revenue growth (+4.5% vs Molina −4.8%), not productivity, so the peer test did not rescue it.
near_misses.materiality: $1.5–$15mm a year on the disclosed 1.5%; 0.012–0.121% of ~$12.4bn annualised SG&A; explains 0.4–4.2% of the 20bp improvement. Below the 0.5% floor by an order of magnitude.
near_misses.watch: Q3/Q4 2026: re-open only on (a) an absolute dollar AI-attributed SG&A saving, or disclosure of the legal spend base that makes "a point and a half" computable, AND (b) SG&A per member per month falling year over year — the test is a print below the $36.14 Q2-2025 baseline. Also watch whether any quantified share of the $480mm optimisation programme is attributed to AI-enabled workflows rather than headcount, and whether AI moves out of the legal department into claims, FWA or member services. A repeat of the legal-only anecdote with no dollar base is confirmation of immateriality, not corroboration.

near_misses.headline: Conveyor automation wearing an AI label — and unit cost went the wrong way

quotes.q: We know that the cost per piece in an automated building is about 28% lower than a non-automated building.
By the end of the second quarter, 68.5% of the volume in our U.S. business was flowing through an automated building compared to 64% one year ago.
Strong base rate growth and increased productivity in our reconfigured network contributed to revenue per piece growing 130 basis points faster than the cost per piece growth rate.

near_misses.kill: The 28%/68.5%/337mm-package evidence is not about artificial intelligence. It describes a UPS facility classification — conveyors, sortation and robotics, 127 automated buildings at end-2025 with 24 more planned — and Tomé's answer to Jordan Aliger (Goldman Sachs) never uses the word AI. The call's four AI references ("AI as the brain", an "AI-powered digital twin", "Our AI is constantly tracking network performance") carry no number, no named system and no baseline; joining them to the 28% is an inference the company never made. The 28% has been stated identically on three consecutive calls (Q4-2025, Q1-2026, Q2-2026), never dated and never reconciled to the segment P&L — a costing constant used to justify capex, not a measured saving. Decisively, unit cost moved the wrong way: revenue per piece +9.3% less the CFO's own 130bp spread implies cost per piece ROSE ~8.0% (adjusted arithmetic +8.5%, GAAP +17.2%) in the very quarter automation penetration rose 4.5pp. The full 100bp US Domestic adjusted margin gain reconciles arithmetically to price over cost, and Dykes' bridge names base rates, customer mix, fuel and "our reconfigured network" — automation and AI appear nowhere in it.
near_misses.survives: UPS has the right SHAPE of disclosure — a repeated cost-per-piece ratio, a tracked penetration series (64% → 66.5% → 68.5%), and a package-equivalent conversion — and it beat its own quantified automation target (68% of US volume by year-end 2026) two quarters early, alongside $3.5bn of 2025 savings delivered and $3bn reaffirmed for 2026. RFID is fully deployed across all US delivery facilities and package cars and the network digital twin is a real system, not vapour. If a number is ever attached to either and it enters the CFO's bridge, UPS becomes a live candidate quickly.
near_misses.materiality: Taken at face value the penetration shift is ~126bp of blended cost per piece, ~$170mm a quarter / ~$690mm annualised against a $13.7bn adjusted US Domestic cost base — material in size, but zero of it currently attributable to AI, and swamped by an 850bp actual increase in cost per piece.
near_misses.watch: Q3 2026 (late Oct): (1) does adjusted cost per piece turn negative year over year — with the Amazon glide-down complete and ~2mm pieces/day gone, Q3 is the first clean read without the volume-deleverage alibi; (2) does the 28% move, get dated or get reconciled — a fourth identical print confirms it as a costing constant and it should be permanently discounted; (3) does automation or AI enter the CFO's margin bridge, which is the admission gate; (4) any number attached to RFID or the digital twin — misload rate, hours per building, planning cycle time. That, not the 28%, would be UPS's first genuine criteria-A datapoint.
near_misses.note: Adversarial reviewer recommended 3 after a −10 promotional-tone and −5 AI-revenue-conflation penalty against a gross of 18. The run analyst recorded the gross 18 and waived both: UPS never claimed the 28% for AI and its AI language is descriptive rather than promotional — the over-reading was the thin screen's, not management's. Either figure is far below the 38 floor; the rejection is unchanged.

near_misses.headline: Reopen denied — a dollar sign newly attached to a decade-old camera platform, and unit cost rose

quotes.q: our Smart Truck platform, which is a combination of artificial intelligence and other forms of technology, certainly, $300 million of run rate EBITDAs is significant.
more than $300 million of annual run rate operating EBITDA through service upgrades, optimized routing, and lower operating costs
That technology on the truck I'm speaking of has been around for probably closer to a decade.
we limited the increase in collection operating costs to less than 1.7% compared to the second quarter of 2025
margin expanded 40 basis points, driven by a strong price to cost spread and continued cost reductions from technology and automation

near_misses.kill: WM was cut on 2026-07-21 for failing the AI-attribution and materiality bar; a cut is not re-litigated without NEW evidence that overcomes the recorded cut reason. The $300m figure is new, but Smart Truck is not: Morris disclosed the platform on the pre-cut Q1-2026 call and dated the hardware to "closer to a decade". The figure is therefore an accumulated program total newly given a run-rate label, not a saving delivered since the cut, and it is arithmetically impossible as an incremental item — $300m is 114bp of margin on FY26 revenue guidance against 40bp of actual margin expansion, inside a 140bp gross line the CFO attributes first to price-to-cost spread while core price runs 6.3% and yield 3.9%. Annualised over the platform's life it is roughly $30m, 0.17% of the $18.2bn opex base, three times below the materiality floor. Attribution fails independently: Fish twice refuses the AI framing ("I don't look at it as just AI"), nobody ever sizes the AI share, and one of the three named benefit sources — "service upgrades" — is revenue capture, not opex. The recycling "30% improvement in labor cost per ton" says automation and never says AI; it is a capex benchmark against legacy facilities. Unit cost moved the wrong way: collection opex +1.7% on volumes -0.4% is +2.1% per unit, and the sub-60% opex ratio is compressed by price in the denominator. Technology appears in the CFO's bridge only as a -40bp HEADWIND, exactly cancelling the +40bp net expansion.
near_misses.survives: WM has a real, decade-matured telematics and imaging estate — every commercial and residential truck outfitted, over 300 million images a year, roughly 95% processed without a human touch — and that is a genuine AI workload at scale. If the company ever decomposes the $300m into an AI-attributable, cost-only figure with a baseline and vintage, WM becomes a live candidate quickly.
near_misses.materiality: $300m against implied FY26 opex of ~$18.2bn is 1.65% as stated, clearing the 0.5% floor on paper. But it is a stock, not a flow: gross EBITDA blending revenue and cost, no accumulation period disclosed, on a platform roughly ten years old. Annualised incrementally it is ~$30m, 0.17% of opex — below the floor by three times.
near_misses.watch: Q3 2026 (late Oct): (1) is the $300m decomposed into AI-versus-cameras/telematics/routing and into service-upgrade revenue versus opex reduction; (2) is a baseline and vintage given so an incremental annual delta can be reconciled to the Collection & Disposal segment P&L; (3) does collection operating cost growth print BELOW volume growth, against this quarter's +1.7% cost on -0.4% volume; (4) does technology move from the headwind side of the CFO's bridge to a named, quantified benefit line. A repeat of "$300 million" unchanged with no reconciliation is confirmation of the UPS costing-constant pattern, not corroboration.
near_misses.note: Peer set is decisive and was run: Clean Harbors posted +190bp of adjusted EBITDA margin — a company-record quarter and a $110m guidance raise — with zero AI attribution, and Waste Connections, whose AI disclosure is genuinely rigorous (seven initiatives, named tools, deployment dates, $100m invested), books just $20m of realized run-rate EBITDA today. WM's unitemized $300m is fifteen times WCN's itemized $20m. Republic Services, Casella and GFL had not published Q2-2026 transcripts in the window.
